title: Shaving or trimming
hook: men shave or trim, women cut a fingertip's length

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sacrifice, and your line: shared meat. Who ended up at your table, or on the other end of a plate? Day one thousand one hundred thirty-five.

"And those who trim?" It's the companions asking. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ has just asked God to have mercy on those who shave their heads. Some of the men listening have only trimmed theirs. So they ask: and those who trim? He repeats the prayer for those who shave. They ask again. Only after asking more than once do they hear him include them: and those who trim. It's a small, almost funny exchange, people making sure they're counted. Today, shaving or trimming.
screen: `MERCY ON THOSE WHO SHAVE.` → `AND THOSE WHO TRIM?` → `AND THOSE WHO TRIM.`

segments.voice: Start with why hair matters here at all. While in ihram, pilgrims don't cut their hair. Surah Al-Baqarah tells them not to shave their heads until the offering has reached its place. So for days, the hair is left alone. Then, after the stoning and the sacrifice, it's cut. Anas reports in Sahih Muslim that the Prophet came back to his place at Mina, called the barber, pointed to one side of his head and then the other, and then gave his hair away to the people. Second, the two ways. The hadith from the hook, in Sahih al-Bukhari, praises those who shave, and when asked, includes those who trim. Both are allowed for men. Shaving is the fuller act; trimming is enough. Third, women. A report from Ibn Abbas in Sunan Abi Dawud says women don't shave; they only shorten. Jurists describe it as cutting about a fingertip's length from the ends. Fourth, what the cut does. It marks a release. With it, much of what ihram held back is lifted, and the pilgrim can wear ordinary clothes again. Surah Al-Fath pictures believers entering the Sacred Mosque in safety, heads shaved and hair cut, without fear. One more thing. On that busy day people did the rites in a jumble, and came to the Prophet worried. One said he'd shaved before sacrificing. The answer, in Bukhari: do it, there's no harm. The schools of law later discussed when a change of order needs making up. But that day, the worried were met with ease. So the end of ihram is something anyone can see: a shaved head, or hair a little shorter at the ends.
screen: `DON'T SHAVE UNTIL THE OFFERING.` · `SHAVE, OR TRIM: BOTH COUNT.` · `WOMEN SHORTEN, NOT SHAVE.` · `A RELEASE FROM IHRAM.` · then, large: `DO IT, THERE'S NO HARM.`

segments.voice: The practice: look at your hands. Settle, and breathe. Turn your hands over, and look at your nails. They've been growing all this time without any help from you, the way a pilgrim's hair grows through ihram. Let that stand for the stretch of time you've just come through, this week, this season. Is there something in it that's finished? Later today, trim your nails, slowly, with the intention of a new start. If you pray, you can begin with bismillah. The bell holds the time.
Shaving or trimming. Men shave or trim their hair, and women cut a little from the ends, marking the release from ihram. Today's word.

Your line: a new start. Today, finish one small thing and mark it, a cut nail, a closed file, a cleared counter, and start the next clean. Tomorrow: the tawaf of Ifadah. Day one thousand one hundred thirty-five.

notes: Bukhari 1727 (also Muslim 1301): mercy for those who shave; the companions ask 'and those who trim?'. The number of repetitions differs between narrations, so no count is given. Confirm.
Muslim 1305 (Anas): the barber, right side then left, hair given to the people. Confirm number.
Abu Dawud 1984/1985 (Ibn Abbas): women do not shave, only shorten. Confirm number and grading. 'About a fingertip's length' is attributed to jurists (from the outline); confirm.
'Much of what ihram held back is lifted' (first tahallul): confirm the phrasing, including what remains restricted until the tawaf of Ifadah.

Bukhari 1736 (or 83/124): 'do it, there's no harm' about rites done out of order. The script notes the schools later discussed when a change of order needs making up (e.g. Hanafi views on dam); confirm wording.
Practice invites bismillah 'if you pray'; no new prayer written.
